title: A Pacific Leaders Meeting with Too Few Leaders
gist: The 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting produced statements but few implementable decisions, with 6 of 18 leaders absent and Naoero and Kiribati again blocking a unified statement naming China over its July 6 submarine-launched ballistic missile test. The Forum created a two-tier partner system that keeps China, the United States and 11 others at the leaders' table, while Beijing's coercion of Palau over Taiwan has cut Chinese tourist arrivals from 91,095 in 2015 to 21,286 in 2025.

themes.theme: Why the Pacific has become contested ground

insights.claim: China's interest in the Pacific is threefold: resources such as fish and lumber, a strategic position that complicates U.S. and allied military planning in a contingency, and reducing Taiwan's diplomatic support abroad.
insights.so_what: A clean three-part lens for reading any Chinese move in the region, including fisheries deals and infrastructure financing.
insights.locator: China’s interest in the Pacific is threefold
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Over the past decade China has secured diplomatic recognition switches from three Pacific states, Kiribati and the Solomon Islands in 2019 and Naoero in late 2024, leaving only the Marshall Islands, Palau and Tuvalu maintaining official ties with Taipei.
insights.so_what: A running count of Taiwan's shrinking diplomatic base; each further switch raises the pressure on Taipei's international standing.
insights.locator: Over the past decade, China has secured the switch
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The year leading into the summit featured China launching its first ever submarine-launched ballistic missile into the Pacific, Australia finalizing mutual defense treaties with Fiji and Papua New Guinea, and a drastic leadership change in the Solomon Islands.
insights.so_what: Three concrete markers that the Pacific security architecture is being rebuilt in real time, with Australia locking in treaty relationships.
insights.locator: The summit comes on the heels of a dynamic year
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Controversies over Taiwan marked both the 2024 and 2025 meetings, with Tonga's 2024 communique rewritten to remove any mention of Taiwan after objections from China's special envoy Qian Bo, and the 2025 Solomon Islands meeting excluding all dialogue partners including the United States, China and Taiwan.
insights.so_what: Establishes a pattern of successful Chinese influence over Forum outputs, which is the benchmark against which 2026 outcomes should be judged.
insights.locator: Both the 2024 and 2025 PIFLMs were marked by controversies
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: This year's Forum produced numerous statements of progress but few actual implementable decisions, with regional issues overshadowed by the geopolitics surrounding the event and the absence of 6 of the 18 leaders.
insights.so_what: Discount Forum communiques as commitments; the gap between statements and implementable decisions is the actual signal.
insights.quote: This year’s forum produced numerous statements of progress on key regional issues, but few actual implementable decisions.
insights.locator: Q2: What were the outcomes of this year’s PIFLM?
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Pacific leaders registered concern over the July 6 intercontinental ballistic missile test that overflew several members without adequate notice and called for at least 24 hours of advance notification, but did not explicitly name China, with Naoero dissociating and Kiribati absent from the leaders' retreat.
insights.so_what: Demonstrates Beijing can reliably veto collective Pacific criticism through two small client states, a durable structural asymmetry.
insights.quote: registered concern on the recent intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) test which overflew a number of Members without adequate notice
insights.locator: One of the more closely watched aspects
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Leaders agreed to sort external partners into two tiers, with China, the United States, Japan, France, India, Indonesia, Germany, the United Kingdom, the European Union, Canada, Singapore, South Korea and the UAE reported as tier-one strategic partners allowed to attend the leaders' meeting, while tier-two sector partners may attend only the foreign ministers meeting.
insights.so_what: Formalizes access to Pacific leaders as a scarce diplomatic asset, and the tier list reveals which powers the region considers strategically material.
insights.locator: The leaders also made progress on a years-long review
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Leaders agreed in principle on the Waqa Moana concept to curb transnational organized crime and illicit drugs, with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announcing $600 million mostly for aerial surveillance of drug vessels and support for Fiji's police force.
insights.so_what: The largest single funding commitment at the summit, showing Australia buying influence through policing and surveillance rather than defense hardware.
insights.locator: In recent years, the Pacific, long a transit hub for drugs
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The Pacific has seen a major uptick in drug trafficking incidents, largely methamphetamine and cocaine destined for Australia and New Zealand.
insights.so_what: Transnational crime, not great power rivalry, is one of the priorities Pacific states themselves name, which shapes what partnerships they will actually value.
insights.locator: In recent years, the Pacific, long a transit hub for drugs
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Forum leaders endorsed the BELAU Declaration calling for keeping the Paris Agreement 1.5 degree goal in reach, centering the ocean-climate nexus, working toward 100 percent renewable energy, and improving climate finance and implementation.
insights.so_what: Climate finance remains the region's price of admission for partners; renewables commitments define where development money will flow.
insights.locator: With climate change continuing to be an existential threat
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The United States sent a delegation led by Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau that announced more than $150 million in regional support, including $60 million for a regional energy security initiative and a feasibility study on Tonga's fuel supply infrastructure.
insights.so_what: The U.S. package is roughly a quarter of Australia's single crime-fighting pledge, a useful measure of relative commitment in the region.
insights.locator: As a PIF dialogue partner, the United States sent a delegation
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: U.S. commitments included $17 million to combat illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, cohosting with Palau the inaugural U.S.-Pacific Islands Conference of Police Ministers, seabed mapping and exploration support, port modernization at Majuro and Ebeye, and telecom and cloud technology assistance.
insights.so_what: Seabed mapping and port modernization are the dual-use investments to watch, with implications for critical minerals and logistics access.
insights.locator: On security cooperation, the United States will provide $17 million
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Several U.S. initiatives were explicitly multilateral, including upgrading Omoka Port in the Cook Islands with New Zealand, developing a new hospital in Palau with Australia, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea and Taiwan, and a drinking water sampling project with Taiwan in Palau.
insights.so_what: Co-financing with Taiwan inside Palau is a deliberate signal that Washington will not let Beijing define Taiwan out of Pacific development work.
insights.locator: The United States also announced initiatives in collaboration
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: One-third of the Forum's leaders were absent, with the heads of Kiribati, Samoa, New Caledonia, Vanuatu, Fiji and the Solomon Islands missing some or all of the discussions at a moment when regional unity was most needed.
insights.so_what: Attendance itself has become a measurable indicator of regional cohesion and of how effectively outside pressure can fragment it.
insights.locator: In a time when regional unity is strongly needed
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale, the most pro-Western leader his country has had in recent years after successive pro-China governments, was forced home hours after arriving in Palau by a no-confidence motion that was withdrawn the day before its scheduled debate, which prevented him from promoting his Blue Pacific Ocean of Peace Regional Security Treaty.
insights.so_what: The timing pattern suggests domestic political instruments can be used to neutralize pro-Western Pacific leaders at critical moments, a recurring risk for Western-aligned governments in the region.
insights.locator: Just a few hours after arriving in Palau
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters suggested outside forces were involved in the leader absences, saying it would be defying gravity and logic to think foreign interference was not to blame, while China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun denied any interference in other countries' internal affairs.
insights.so_what: A senior allied government openly alleging interference raises the diplomatic temperature and signals more overt Western counter-pressure ahead.
insights.quote: it would be “defying gravity and logic” to think that foreign interference was not to blame for multiple leader absences
insights.locator: Given that Wale is the most pro-Western leader
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Kiribati President Taaneti Maamau claimed he could not secure a flight and sent Kiribati's director of foreign service and former ambassador to China in his place, who also skipped the leaders' retreat and was initially not announced at the closing ceremony.
insights.so_what: The substitution choice and the retreat absence are the tell for where Kiribati's alignment sits, useful for predicting future Forum vetoes.
insights.locator: Kiribati President Taaneti Maamau claimed he could not attend
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Chinese tourist arrivals to Palau fell from 91,095 in 2015 to 21,286 in 2025 as Beijing restricted state-backed tour groups and repeatedly issued travel warnings, including an August 19 advisory citing theft and robbery targeting tourists.
insights.so_what: A quantified case study of weaponized tourism: a roughly 77 percent collapse in arrivals is the measurable cost of maintaining ties with Taipei.
insights.locator: China has long taken issue with Taiwan’s position
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Taiwan's embassy in Palau condemned China's attempts to politicize and weaponize tourism, and the U.S. embassy in Koror publicly opposed Chinese efforts to weaponize tourism to coerce Palau and called on Beijing to cease all coercive activities.
insights.so_what: Washington now explicitly names economic coercion in the Pacific, a template it may extend to other small states facing Chinese pressure.
insights.locator: Taiwan’s embassy in Palau issued a response
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs pressured Forum Secretary General Baron Waqa on August 11 to strictly adhere to the one-China principle, and after Taiwan Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung participated in side events China's Pacific envoy Qian Bo warned there will always be consequences.
insights.so_what: Explicit threat language directed at the Forum secretariat is the mechanism to watch for whether Taiwan keeps its development-partner status.
insights.quote: There will always be consequences . . . this should not have happened. We think it’s very inappropriate.
insights.locator: Q5: How did tensions around China and Taiwan play out
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: With New Zealand hosting next year's Forum meeting, Beijing's actions are unlikely to prevent Taiwan's participation again as a development partner, though attempts to manipulate the Forum's posture on Taiwan and to mute regional responses to actions such as the missile test will likely continue.
insights.so_what: Host-country identity is the swing variable for Taiwan's Pacific access, making the 2027 and later host rotations worth tracking.
insights.locator: Conclusion
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Growing outside attention could bring more resources to the Pacific but also risks overshadowing the priorities Pacific nations have actually defined for themselves, namely climate change, economic security and transnational crime, and the partners best positioned to earn lasting influence will be those willing to invest in those priorities rather than in great power competition.
insights.so_what: A practical test for which outside power gains durable Pacific influence: alignment with locally defined priorities beats security-framed spending.
insights.locator: Conclusion
insights.speaker: CSIS
